# Sampling and quantisation

*Lecture 1 · EEU 08101 Control Engineering Digital Analysis*

## Sampling

**Sampling** is measuring the value of a continuous-time signal at uniform intervals, which turns it into a discrete-time sequence:

$$x(k) = x(kT_s), \qquad k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$$

where $T_s$ is the **sampling period** and $f_s = 1/T_s$ is the **sampling frequency**.

The ADC reads the continuous signal x(t) every T seconds, giving the sequence x(k) = x(kT). Between the instants the controller knows nothing about x(t).</figcaption></figure>

**Why sample at all?**

- Digital controllers (microprocessors, DSPs, PLCs) cannot process continuous signals.
- Sensors produce continuous signals, so these must be sampled and digitised first.
- After processing, the output goes back to the plant through a DAC.

**Types of sampling:**

- **Uniform** (the usual case): samples at fixed, regular intervals. This makes analysis and implementation easier.
- **Non-uniform:** samples at irregular intervals. It is used in special cases, such as event-driven control.

## Aliasing

If a signal is sampled **too slowly**, its high-frequency components appear in the samples as **lower** frequencies. This is **aliasing**, and it distorts the signal. *Everyday example:* video recorded at only 10 frames per second makes fast motion look jerky, and wheels can even seem to turn backwards.

text-anchor="middle" class="d-t s m">0.5</text><text x="566" y="202" text-anchor="end" class="d-t s m">9 Hz signal (thin), samples at 10 Hz (dots), apparent 1 Hz signal (red)</text></svg><figcaption>Aliasing. A 9 Hz cosine sampled at only 10 Hz (well below its Nyquist rate of 18 Hz) gives exactly the same samples as a 1 Hz cosine. After sampling the two cannot be told apart, so the controller would see a slow 1 Hz signal that is not there.</figcaption></figure>

Once a signal has been sampled, an alias cannot be removed, because the samples are identical. The only cure is to prevent it: sample fast enough, and filter out frequencies above $f_s/2$ **before** sampling.

## The Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem

A band-limited signal whose highest frequency is $f_{max}$ can be **perfectly reconstructed** from its samples if

$$\boxed{f_s \ge 2f_{max}}$$

(strictly, $f_s > 2f_{max}$). The minimum rate $2f_{max}$ is the **Nyquist rate**, and $f_s/2$ is the **Nyquist frequency**: the highest frequency the samples can represent.

*Example:* a signal containing frequencies up to 1 kHz needs $f_s \ge 2 \times 1000 = 2$ kHz. In practice engineers use $f_s = 5$ to $10 \times f_{max}$.

**Practical guidelines for control:**

1. Find the bandwidth (the highest frequency of interest) of the plant or closed loop.
2. Choose $f_s$ at least **10 times the closed-loop bandwidth** (a rule of thumb).
3. Always put an **anti-aliasing filter** (an analog low-pass filter) before the ADC, so that high-frequency noise cannot fold down into the band of interest.

### Worked questions

**Q1.** $x(t) = \sin(200\pi t)$ is sampled every $T_s = 1$ ms. Find $f_s$ and check the Nyquist criterion.

$f_s = 1/0.001 = 1000$ Hz. From $\omega = 2\pi f = 200\pi$, the signal frequency is $f = 100$ Hz, so the Nyquist rate is 200 Hz. Since $1000 \ge 200$, the criterion is met, with 10 samples per cycle.

**Q2.** A signal contains frequencies up to 1.2 kHz and is sampled at 1.5 kHz. What happens?

The Nyquist rate is 2.4 kHz, and 1.5 kHz is below it, so **aliasing** occurs. The Nyquist frequency is only 750 Hz, so every component between 750 Hz and 1.2 kHz folds back to $|f - f_s|$. For example, a 1.2 kHz component appears at $1.5 - 1.2 = 0.3$ kHz.

**Q3.** A system has a closed-loop bandwidth of 80 Hz. Recommend a sampling range. What happens at only 100 Hz?

At 5 to 10 times the bandwidth, $f_s = 400$ to 800 Hz; the stricter 10× rule gives at least 800 Hz. At 100 Hz the Nyquist frequency is 50 Hz, below the 80 Hz bandwidth. The loop's own signals would alias, and the controller would act on false, low-frequency information. Expect poor performance and possibly instability.

## Quantisation

**Quantisation** maps the continuous range of amplitudes onto a **finite set of levels**, so that each sample can be stored as a number. Sampling discretises time; quantisation discretises amplitude.

An $n$-bit ADC has $2^n$ levels. The step size is

$$\Delta = \frac{V_{max} - V_{min}}{2^n}$$

*Example:* a 3-bit ADC over 0 to 8 V has $2^3 = 8$ levels and $\Delta = \dfrac{8 - 0}{8} = 1$ V. Rounding to the nearest level:

- 0.3 V → 0 V;
- 2.6 V → 3 V;
- 7.2 V → 7 V.

style="fill:var(--red)"/><text x="444.40000000000003" y="58" text-anchor="middle" class="d-t s r">7.2 V → 7</text></svg><figcaption>A 3-bit ADC over 0–8 V: 2³ = 8 levels, Δ = 1 V apart. Each input is rounded to the nearest level (0.3 V → 0, 2.6 V → 3, 7.2 V → 7) and then encoded as a 3-bit word. The dashed line is the ideal input; the gap between it and the staircase is the quantisation error, at most ±Δ/2.</figcaption></figure>

**Quantisation error.** This is the difference between the actual and the quantised value:

$$e_q = x_{actual} - x_{quantised}, \qquad |e_q| \le \frac{\Delta}{2}$$

A smaller step gives a smaller error. In the example the errors are +0.3 V, −0.4 V and +0.2 V, all within ±0.5 V.

**Resolution.** This is the step size as a fraction of the full range:

$$\text{resolution} = \frac{1}{2^n} \times 100\%$$

| ADC | Levels | Resolution |
|---|---|---|
| 3-bit | 8 | 12.5% |
| 8-bit | 256 | 0.39% |
| 12-bit | 4096 | 0.024% |

More bits give finer resolution and a more accurate digital representation.

## Encoding

**Encoding** writes each quantised level as a binary code word of $n$ bits. In the 3-bit example, level 3 is stored as 011 and level 7 as 111. That word is what the controller actually processes.
